docs.title: About
docs.text:
About

About Me

Computer Science student, CTF player, and occasional writer of overly long writeups.

Hi, I'm Siddharth Mathur, a Computer Science student passionate about Cyber Security, Reverse Engineering, Binary Exploitation, Web Security, Digital Forensics, Cryptography, and CTF competitions.

I created this website to document my learning journey through CTF writeups. Every challenge teaches something new, and these notes serve both as my personal knowledge base and as a resource for others working through similar problems.

docs.title: What you'll find here
docs.text:
• Structured writeups — approach, tooling, and the reasoning behind each step, not just the final flag.
  • Reusable techniques — patterns that show up across categories: crypto reductions, binary exploitation primitives, forensic triage, and web exploitation chains.
  • Honest notes on what didn't work — the dead ends are often as instructive as the solution.

docs.title: Recon

README.md
# MyGit

### If you want the flag, make sure to push the flag!

Only flag.txt pushed by ```root:root@picoctf``` will be updated with the flag.

GOOD LUCK!

We need to change the username to root and email to root@picoctf and push a file named flag.txt to get the flag

docs.title: Exploitation Strategy
docs.text:
1. Change the Username to root
  2. Change the email to root@picoctf
  3. create a empty .txt file with name flag.txt
  4. commit and puch it to the main branch

docs.text:
The challenge provides a small python program and nd asks us to connect to a remote service

app.py
while(True):

docs.title: Challenge Overview
docs.text:
In this challenge we need to connect to a netcat server and reveres the given string to get the flag, On connecting to the given netcat address the instruction provided are:

===Welcome to the Text Transformations Challenge!===

Your goal: step by step, recover the original flag.
At each step, you'll see the transformed flag and a hint.
Enter the correct Linux command to reverse the last transformation.

docs.title: Step 1: Base64 reverse
docs.text:
Current flag: KTBxcDI0bnIwLWZhMDFnQHplMHNmYTRlRy1nazNnLXRhMWZlcmlyRShTR1BicHZj
Hint: Base64 encoded the string.
Enter the Linux command to reverse it:

Linux command to reverse base64 is:

base64 -d

docs.title: Step 2: Reversing the string
docs.text:
Current flag: )0qp24nr0-fa01g@ze0sfa4eG-gk3g-ta1ferirE(SGPbpvc
Hint: Reversed the text.
Enter the Linux command to reverse it:
Linux command to reverse is:

rev

docs.title: Step 3:Replacing Dashes
docs.text:
Current flag: cvpbPGS(Eriref1at-g3kg-Ge4afs0ez@g10af-0rn42pq0)
Hint: Replaced underscores with dashes.
Enter the Linux command to reverse it:
To replace tokens we use 'tr' command in linux. The command to replace underscores with dashes is:

tr '-' '_'

docs.title: step 4: Replacing braces
docs.text:
Current flag: cvpbPGS(Eriref1at_g3kg_Ge4afs0ez@g10af_0rn42pq0)
Hint: Replaced curly braces with parentheses.
Enter the Linux command to reverse it:

We will use 'tr' again:

tr '()' '{}'

docs.title: Step 5: Reversing ROT13
docs.text:
Current flag: cvpbPGS{Eriref1at_g3kg_Ge4afs0ez@g10af_0rn42pq0}
Hint: Applied ROT13 to letters.
Enter the Linux command to reverse it:
ROT13 can be reversed using Linux command:

tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
• Base64 encoded string can be decoded using 'base64 -d'
  • Any string can be reversed using 'rev'
  • To replace tokens in a string we use 'tr'
  • ROT13 can be reversed using tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m
